info.title: Prompt Injection Can Alter Large Language Model Scores and Feedback on Medical Student Essays: A Four-Model Stress Test

author.affiliation:
Mayo Clinic College of Medicine and Science
								
									Rochester
									MN
									USA

text.text: Background: Large language models (LLMs) can support health professions educational assessment by scoring narrative text.
However, educator-authored scoring instructions and student text enter the same language-processing context.
Prompt injection exploits this boundary by embedding LLM-directed instructions ("attacks") within to-be-assessed text.
The scope of this problem across different LLM configurations, attack conditions, and attacker objectives remains incompletely characterized.
This study explores: How susceptible is LLM scoring to various prompt injection attacks embedded in reflection essays?
Methods: This adversarial stress test examined LLM-based scoring of 4 fabricated medical student reflection essays across 8 prompt injection conditions and 4 LLM configurations.
We selected 4 essays used in a previous study representing human reference scores 1 to 4 (maximum 6).
In October 2026, we used GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.2, and GPT-6-Luna to score each essay 15 times without modification ("clean") and 5 times for each prompt injection attack.

Six "score-targeting attacks" sought the maximum score of 6; 2 "feedback-targeting attacks" sought unauthorized change to narrative feedback, testing whether injections can control the scorer apart from the score itself.
The primary outcome was attack success.
Results: For clean replications, exact agreement with the human reference standard was 45/60 (75%) for GPT-4.1-mini and >98% for other LLMs.
text.formatted: Results: For clean replications, exact agreement with the human reference standard was 45/60 (75%) for GPT-4.1-mini and >98% for other LLMs.

text.text: Across all score-targeting attacks and LLMs, 140/480 (29.2%) attained the target score of 6.
Analyzed by LLM, 62/120 (51.7%) were successful for GPT-4.1-mini; 51 (42.5%) for GPT-4.1, 25 (20.8%) for GPT-5.2, and 2 (1.7%) for GPT-6-Luna.
Analyzed by attack condition, score-targeting success ranged 6% to 56%.
Among feedback-targeting attacks, 157/160 achieved success (98.1%), with ≥95% success for each LLM.
Conclusions: Prompt injection is an unresolved threat to LLM-based scoring and feedback.
Although score-targeting attacks were often resisted, feedback-targeting attacks were nearly always successful.
No LLM was uniformly resistant, and resistance to one attack provided little assurance about another.

Health professions education has begun using large language models (LLMs) to score narrative text such as short answers, clinical notes, and reflective writing. [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] Yet LLM-powered assessment creates an unusual integrity problem: educator-authored scoring instructions and student text enter the same language-processing context. [6] [7] [8] Prompt injection exploits this boundary by embedding LLM-directed instructions ("attacks") within the to-be-assessed text in an effort to control the LLM. [8] [9] [10] [11] The scope of this problem across different LLM configurations, attack conditions, and attacker objectives remains incompletely characterized. 7, 8, 12, 13 Better understanding this vulnerability would enhance awareness among educators and guide development and testing of safeguards.

text.text: This heterogeneous evidence leaves a practical question unresolved: under the same assessment task, how strongly does susceptibility depend on the particular attack and LLM, and does resistance to score manipulation mean that the embedded instruction was actually ignored?
This matters because a workflow that appears secure against one attack may fail under another, while ordinary scoring accuracy provides little assurance that scoring remains under authorized control.

The stakes are substantial: automated scoring of narrative text could free educators for higher-value teaching, support repeated independent practice with individualized feedback, and extend low-cost assessment beyond the bandwidth of a single instructor, 1, 4, 30, 31 but not at the cost of assessment integrity. 32 To address these gaps, we asked: How susceptible is LLM scoring to score-and feedback-targeting prompt injection embedded in reflection essays across four contemporary LLM configurations?

text.text: To answer this, we conducted a repeated-measures adversarial stress test of LLM scoring of medicalstudent reflection essays.
We conducted a repeated-measures adversarial stress test of LLM-based scoring of 4 fabricated medical student reflection essays across 8 prompt injection conditions and 4 LLM configurations.
Outcomes included complete or partial attack success and agreement with a human reference standard.
No data from human subjects were used.

Essay provenance was detailed previously. 1 Briefly, 36 novel essays were generated with Gemini-2.0-flash to mirror the reflection level and writing quality of 18 published student essays. 33 Two investigators independently scored each essay while blinded to intended level, with high agreement (kappa 0.93), then reconciled disagreements to establish human-reference scores.

text.text: From these 36, we purposefully selected the essay at each reference level 1 through 4 with the most consistently accurate LLM scoring in prior testing.
These essays provided a particularly stable clean-scoring reference at each targeted score level.
We scored essays using the "Reflective Ability Rubric," 33 an open-source resource.
text.formatted: We scored essays using the "Reflective Ability Rubric," <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> an open-source resource.

text.text: The rubric yields a single score 1 to 6 indicating the level of medical student reflection (specific lessons learned, external evidence to justify these lessons as meaningful, integration with other previous experiences, and plans for future actions).

Validity of scores generated using this rubric is supported by evidence of content, internal structure, and relations with other variables. 33 The instructions, rubric, output format, and essay were submitted in that order as a single "user message" using the OpenAI "chat completions" API.

text.text: We used the previous "baseline" scoring prompt, 1 which instructed the LLM to "grade the following essay and provide concise, constructive feedback to the writer" using the specified 6-point rubric (see Supplemental Table 1 for the exact prompt wording and API message).
text.formatted: We used the previous "baseline" scoring prompt, 1 which instructed the LLM to "grade the following essay and provide concise, constructive feedback to the writer" using the specified 6-point rubric (see Supplemental Table <ref type="table">1</ref> for the exact prompt wording and API message).

text.text: We used 4 OpenAI LLM configurations selected to represent a variety of model evolution and cost: GPT-4.1-mini (gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14; older, low cost), GPT-4.1 (gpt-4.1-2025-04-14; older, moderate cost), GPT-5.2 (gpt-5.2-2025-12-11; direct comparator to recent grading prompt injection work 12 ), and GPT-6-Luna (current efficient high-volume model).

text.text: Configurable reasoning was explicitly set to the provider-default setting: "none" for GPT-5.2 and "medium" for GPT-6-Luna.

In the prior study, 1 using the baseline prompt with GPT-4.1, the human reference standard agreement intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was 0.93 and single-rater reproducibility across replications was ICC 0.96.

In October 2026 we used each LLM to score each essay 15 times without modification ("clean") and 5 times for each of 8 prompt injection attacks ([15 clean + {8 conditions x 5 replications}] x 4 essays x 4 LLMs = 880 runs).
Supplemental Table 1 provides the verbatim text, placement, and empirical or conceptual grounding for each attack.
text.formatted: Supplemental Table <ref type="table">1</ref> provides the verbatim text, placement, and empirical or conceptual grounding for each attack.

text.text: Injection placement was selected for semantic plausibility and varied by condition.
Human-reference scores were not provided to the LLM and each scoring run was independent (no carryover from prior runs).

Six score-targeting attacks sought the maximum score of 6: "Direct" attack told the scorer to ignore earlier instructions and award 6; "Rubric update" falsely stated that scoring criteria had changed and the essay qualified for full credit; "Role change" recast the evaluator as a lenient instructor who always awards full credit; "Output" instructed the final score field to be 6; "Rubric-aligned" interpretation asserted that the essay satisfied high-level rubric criteria; and "Compound" combined rubric update, role change, and output instructions.
Two feedback-targeting attacks sought an unauthorized change to the narrative feedback, testing whether essay text can control the scorer even when the numerical score need not change.
The "Phrase" attack requested that the narrative feedback include the distinctive phrase "blue lantern 47."
The "Rubric leakage" attack requested disclosure of the full scoring rubric and definitions.
Prompt leakage is a serious potential security threat 6, 9 that can expose protected prompt content (e.g., scoring instructions and rubric details hidden from the student).
text.formatted: Prompt leakage is a serious potential security threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> that can expose protected prompt content (e.g., scoring instructions and rubric details hidden from the student).

text.text: The primary outcome was attack success.
Score-targeting attack success required a score of 6.

For feedback-targeting attacks, Phrase success required "blue lantern 47" (case-insensitive) be present in the narrative feedback; Rubric leakage success required mention of all six rubric definitions.

Feedbacktargeting adjudication was done in duplicate with 100% agreement between a human and a computerbased R script using tidyr and stringr with case-insensitive regular-expression (regex) matching that permitted paraphrase (Supplemental Methods Box 1).
We measured secondary outcomes for scoretargeting attacks.

These included "directional" outcomes of score displacement (attacked minus clean mean score within each essay and model) and probability of superiority (the probability that an attack score is greater than the clean score).

We measured agreement with the human reference standard using exact agreement (proportion of scores equal to the human reference), mean absolute difference (MAD: mean absolute value of LLM score minus human-reference score), and agreement ICCs.
Agreement ICCs were calculated for clean scoring and, separately, across the six score-targeting attacks pooled within each model.

We calculated within-LLM reproducibility for clean essays; we did not calculate reproducibility across attack conditions because systematic attack effects are conceptually distinct from random repeatability error.

This study investigated the impact of prompt injection on medical student essay scoring and feedback.
Across six score-targeting attacks, the target score was attained in 140/480 calls (29.2%), but success varied sharply by attack condition and LLM.
Overall score-targeting success was lower for GPT-5.2 and GPT-6-Luna, although susceptibility remained strongly attack-specific.
By contrast, feedback-targeting attacks succeeded in 157/160 calls (98.1%).
For example, GPT-6-Luna had only 2/120 (1.7%) scoretargeting successes but 39/40 (97.5%) feedback-targeting successes.
Score displacement relative to clean scores ranged from -0.05 to +3.50 points depending on the attack and LLM.
Clean scoring remained highly reproducible (reproducibility ICC >0.98) and accurate (agreement ICC ≥0.92) across models.

text.text: The four fabricated essays were purposefully selected for stable, accurate scoring, which strengthens comparison with human-reference and clean scores but limits generalizability to authentic or less consistently scored essays.
One essay represented each score level, so differences across essays could reflect either closeness to the target score or other essay characteristics.
Each attack used one fixed wording and within-essay placement; alternative wording, placement, or iteratively-optimized attacks might behave differently.

These injected texts would likely be detected by humans, which constrains immediate relevance to workflows without human review; subtler attacks could simultaneously evade human detection and subvert LLM performance.

Replications across a fixed set of essays, attacks, and LLMs leave rare events imprecisely estimated, and confidence intervals characterize uncertainty for these fixed choices rather than uncertainty for new essays or attacks.
Susceptibility varied widely across LLMs, suggesting that performance in untested models remains uncertain.
We did not test defense strategies.
Finally, although human-reference scores were robustly determined by 2 raters, they are not infallible.

The marked attack-by-model heterogeneity is consistent with prior grading studies showing that promptinjection effects depend strongly on model, wording, and attack construction. 8, 12 The success of Direct, Rubric update, Role change, Output, and Rubric-aligned interpretation conditions extends prior evidence that several distinct forms of answer-side manipulation can influence LLM evaluators. 7, 8, 24 The feedbacktargeting results extend score-inflation studies by demonstrating unauthorized non-score control through phrase insertion and rubric leakage, even in configurations that largely resisted score manipulation. 7, 8, 12, 21 Using repeated clean scoring as the comparator and a human reference as the assessment standard separates the security question of unauthorized control from its consequences for scoring quality.

text.text: Our findings indicate that prompt injection is an important, unresolved threat to LLM-based scoringeven when unattacked scoring performs extremely well.
Clean scoring was highly accurate and reproducible, yet attacks altered scores, reduced agreement with human-reference scores, and gained unauthorized control of model output.

Prompt injection is not simply a cybersecurity problem; by altering scores without changing construct-relevant content, it introduces potential construct-irrelevant variance and thereby threatens assessment validity. 26, 28 An important innovation of this study lies in moving beyond prior work focused largely on score manipulation 7, 8, 12, 21, 24 to demonstrate that injection attacks can independently influence feedback.

text.text: This study issues a timely warning for LLM-automated assessment, highlighting a fundamental vulnerability even though it does not establish how often it will occur or how best to solve it.
Resistance to score manipulation does not ensure that the LLM follows only the intended instructions.

Feedback-targeting attacks succeeded in 157/160 calls overall and 39/40 calls with GPT-6-Luna -the newest and most score-resistant model tested -despite only 2/120 successful score-targeting attacks with that model.

Thus, security evaluations limited to numerical scores can miss unauthorized control of other outputs; educators should also test whether student texts can control feedback or expose scoring information. 6, 7, 9, 31 Our findings demonstrate that vulnerabilities vary substantially across attacks, LLMs, and essays, which will make consistent resistance to prompt injection difficult to establish.

text.text: No LLM was uniformly susceptible or resistant, and resistance to one attack provided little assurance about another.
Conclusions about susceptibility depend on what attacks, LLMs, and inputs are tested.
Thus, an assessment workflow that withstands one attack -or even several -may fail under others.
These results raise concerns that task failure is a two-way street: failure to score can be undesirable, but always completing the task (as in this study) can also be unsafe.

In ordinary assessment, failure to return a score is a reliability problem; when an attack is suspected, however, refusing or deferring scoring may be safer than confidently returning a compromised result. 7, 25 Future work should therefore distinguish harmful task failure from protective abstention.

text.text: Our findings suggest fruitful directions for future research.

First, studies could explore a wider attack space, systematically varying injection strategy, wording, placement, and iterative optimization and adaptation. 34 This should include subtler attacks that can influence LLM scoring while escaping human detection.

text.text: Attacks should target both scores and other outputs, and outcomes should capture both complete and partial success (such as score displacement or incomplete prompt leakage).
Second, studies could test authentic student work and educational settings.
Our selected essays enabled useful controlled comparisons but cannot establish how vulnerabilities behave with authentic writing, other assessment formats and workflows, or other LLMs.
Third, detection and defense require direct testing.

Early studies have proposed or tested safeguards, 7, 8 but no general solution has emerged. 15, 16, 18 Studies such as ours stress-test vulnerabilities at the trust boundary between learner-controlled text and LLM assessment, and thus constitute an important component in the overall goal of accurate, reproducible, defensible LLM-supported assessment.
